summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory under Moroccan military administration, and a visitor there stands under Morocco's penal code wherever Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate. Human Rights Watch documented that authority in a dispatch of 9 December 2005, covering the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under that framework and carries six months to three years of imprisonment, and the broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. A July 2017 PinkNews global legality roundup lists it as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and records that it has been illegal there for decades, with a status of criminalised. The Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA describe same-sex sexual activity as illegal in the SADR for both males and females, punishable by up to three years in prison.

Where Sahrawi government officials administer refugee camps in Algeria, a 2009 USCRI report found officials saying they were holding some prisoners on homosexuality charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, so a trans visitor outside Moroccan-controlled areas has no sourced protection machinery to rely on either.

The SADR's own legal position is contested. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it, a statement that sits against the criminalisation recorded by the monitoring catalogues; CEAR concludes that the ambiguity leaves no legal protection for LGBTQ people against discrimination or violence.
tangentialFactors:
Western Sahara was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalized in Spain until 1979, shaping the legal and social inheritance of the territory. The inherited statutory line runs through Morocco as well: same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the SADR claims, so the criminalising default a visitor encounters is common to both claimant administrations.

Most residents of the territory are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon. That social climate is not itself an offence, but it bears on the risk of reporting violence and on the reception a visibly trans visitor can expect from neighbours and local officials alike.
localsOnly:
Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria were found by USCRI in 2009 to be holding prisoners on homosexuality charges in cases where the alleged facts would more fittingly describe rape, indicating that the charge is available to camp authorities as a dispositional tool rather than a narrowly drawn offence.

Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, stated in 2010 that the Constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it. CEAR concludes from that silence that Sahrawi law provides no protection against discrimination or violence, so residents who are targeted have no domestic remedy.

Sahrawi activists inside Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara face prosecution by Moroccan courts, as in the 2005 trial of seven human-rights defenders whom Human Rights Watch believed were charged on dubious grounds, and detention has followed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses trans-specific law: legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, restroom or facility access, access to hormone therapy or transition-related care, and hate-crime aggravation are all unsourced for Western Sahara under either administration, so a visitor cannot rely on the record for those questions.

The SADR's constitutional position on same-sex conduct is unresolved: the monitoring catalogues record criminalisation with up to three years' imprisonment while a 2010 senior diplomatic statement denies that the Constitution punishes it, and no primary statutory text is available here to settle which reading governs in practice.

The Moroccan penalty range of six months to three years, and the PinkNews and monitoring-catalogue figures derived from it, are carried from secondary reporting rather than quoted from the penal code itself in this inventory. The Algerian law governing the refugee camps where SADR officials hold detainees is likewise not sourced, as is the screening practice applied to trans travellers at border crossings.
